data.title: Is SOFI Stock a Buy after a 35% Drop? Here's What Wall Street Expects
data.description:
SoFi Technologies (SOFI) has declined 35% year-to-date amid concerns about the fintech company's growing reliance on its lending business, which has high capital requirements and is exposed to credit risk, especially in a challenging macro backdrop. Wall Street is currently divided on SOFI stock. While SoFi bulls point to strong fundamentals and continued growth in its member base, other analysts worry about risks tied to higher interest rates and the rising share of lending business.

Analysts Are Divided on SOFI Stock

Earlier this month, Loop Capital analyst Reginald Smith initiated coverage of SOFI stock with a price target of $22. The 4-star analyst highlighted that SoFi is a leading digital bank with a broad product range and the best client-acquisition and deposit-gathering platform among mid-size banks.  

While Smith expects SoFi to deliver low- to mid-20% compound annual growth rates (CAGR) for revenue and EBITDA in 2027 and 2028, he prefers to be on the sidelines amid the risk of interest rate hikes and the mix shift toward the more asset-intensive lending business. The analyst sees this shift as the correct strategy for the long term, but expects it to impact SOFI stock over the near term.

The analyst views SoFi Technologies as one of the most "compelling long-term investments" in his coverage. Jeffrey noted that while secular growth companies, like crypto infrastructure providers, await regulatory clarity and institutional adoption, SoFi is gaining market share in the well-established consumer finance market, which he believes is well-positioned for disruption.

Jeffrey contends that while short-term investors may worry about a lack of catalysts amid rising interest rates and revenue-mix concerns, he remains bullish due to SOFI's more than $25 billion total addressable market (TAM), extensive scale, and attractive risk/reward profile.

Is SOFI Stock a Good Buy Now?

data.title: GameStop (GME) Turnaround Looks More Convincing with Insider Buying
data.description:
GameStop (GME) is showing signs of a turnaround, and insider buying makes the case more convincing. Unlike other stocks with similar name recognition, GameStop has no formal analyst rating as of September 19, 2026. The stock has lost roughly 15% over the past year as the S&P 500 (SPX) gained more than 15%.

By most measures, Wall Street has already moved on from GameStop, or at least decided it isn't worth discussing. Yet while Wall Street was looking in the other direction, something has changed inside GameStop. The company's gross margins have expanded from 29.1% to 43.7% in 12 months. Operating income has doubled to a record $160.2 million, while earnings per share (EPS) have grown 145.76%, which is a huge turnaround after years of losses.

Perhaps most notable is that CEO Ryan Cohen is once again signaling his commitment to the business by indicating he bought another one million shares totaling $20.3 million. His purchase at $20.38 per share shows real faith in GameStop's turnaround and new focus on collectibles, regardless of Wall Street's interest. This is why the GameStop story is still interesting, and why I'm bullish on the stock.

data.title: S&P 500 Earnings Jump 51% as Goldman Says Profits Are Running Above Trend
data.description:
S&P 500 (SPY) companies are earning far more than usual. However, Goldman Sachs (GS) does not think that this is another dot-com-style earnings bubble. Earnings per share for the S&P 500 jumped by 51% year-over-year in Q2 2026 and have risen by 26% over the past four quarters. That pace has only been surpassed during the post-recession rebounds of 2010 and 2021. Still, valuations look less extreme when using future earnings.

The S&P 500's forward P/E has fallen from 23x a year ago to 19x today, which matches its 10-year average. Goldman believes that three temporary forces explain much of the unusual profit growth.

The first is the AI investment boom. Amazon (AMZN) and Meta (META) are part of a group of major technology companies expected to spend about $800 billion on capital expenditures this year. Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL) are also included. That total is up 94% from 2025.

Promotion

200% short exposure to AMZN with AMZO

Goldman estimates that this spending accounts for nearly half of S&P 500 EPS growth this year. However, the firm expects the boost to fade as spending growth slows down and depreciation costs rise.

Chip Margins and Investment Gains Are Also Boosting Earnings

Separately, semiconductor profits are another major factor. Memory companies are currently seeing gross margins that are near 80%, more than twice their historical average.

Goldman estimates that higher margins explain about one-quarter of semiconductor earnings growth this year. If overall chip gross margins fall from roughly 70% today to their 15-year average of 55%, Goldman estimates that S&P 500 earnings could fall by about 10%.

Investment gains are also temporarily lifting reported profits. Large technology companies generated more than $150 billion of "other income" from private investment gains in Q2. That represented roughly 12% of S&P 500 EPS.

Goldman expects these gains to shrink substantially in 2027, which could reduce year-over-year earnings growth by about eight percentage points.

Still, even after these temporary boosts fade, Goldman expects S&P 500 EPS to grow by 11% in 2027 to $415. Another 11% increase could take earnings to $460 in 2028. The firm expects AI productivity to add roughly one to two percentage points to growth and maintains a 12-month S&P 500 target of 8,700, or about 14% above the level used in its analysis.

data.title: Amazon Faces EU Scrutiny Over Rules That Could Limit Lower Prices Elsewhere
data.description:
E-commerce giant Amazon (AMZN) is facing new scrutiny from the European Commission over whether its marketplace rules make it harder for third-party sellers to charge lower prices elsewhere. According to Bloomberg, regulators have contacted sellers about so-called price-parity restrictions. These practices could potentially hurt merchants if Amazon reduces the visibility of products that are sold for less on a rival marketplace or the seller's own website. The review is still in its early stages, so regulators have not found that Amazon violated EU rules.

The issue matters because Amazon Marketplace is already covered by the EU's Digital Markets Act, or DMA. Article 5(3) of the law prevents designated gatekeepers from stopping businesses from offering the same products through other channels at different prices or conditions.

However, one seller contacted during the EU review said that if his company sells the product for less on its own website, Amazon can reduce its visibility on Amazon Marketplace. In his view, that gives Amazon influence over what sellers charge elsewhere.

EU Review Could Become a Formal Investigation

For now, the European Commission is gathering information rather than formally accusing Amazon of wrongdoing. Still, the review could become a full investigation if regulators find evidence that Amazon's practices are hurting competition.

Interestingly, similar pricing concerns have already attracted regulatory attention. In February, Germany's competition regulator ordered Amazon to stop certain marketplace pricing practices and repay €59 million in economic benefits. EU lawmakers later questioned whether those practices could also violate Article 5(3) of the DMA.

Nevertheless, the European Commission says that it remains in regular discussions with Amazon and its business customers in order to monitor whether it is complying with the rule. Meanwhile, Amazon says it is committed to following the DMA and that it continues to cooperate with the Commission's regulatory oversight.

data.title: Market Wrap: Stocks End a Volatile Week as Interest Rates and Treasury Yields Move Higher
data.description:
U.S. equities were little changed on Sept. 18, ending a volatile trading week as interest rates and Treasury yields moved higher and the Iran war continued to upend crude oil prices. The major stock averages ended mixed for the week. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 2% on the week. The S&P 500 was lower by about 0.3% while the technology-heavy Nasdaq ended up 0.3%.

Markets closed out an up-and-down trading week in which investors navigated another rise in Treasury yields and oil prices, along with the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hike in three years. U.S. stocks plunged on Sept. 16 after the central bank lifted its trendsetting Fed Funds Rate by 25 basis points. However, equities rallied hard the following day to erase most of the previous session's losses.

Rising Treasury Yields and Oil Prices

Also contributing to the week's volatility were rising Treasury yields and crude oil prices. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note was back above 5% on Sept. 18, its highest level since 2007. At the same time, crude oil prices climbed above $100 this week. Brent crude, the international standard, neared $110 a barrel before pulling back to trade around $104.

data.title: Paramount Skydance (NASDAQ:PSKY) Stock Slides After FCC Approves 49.5% Foreign Ownership Stake
data.description:
Entertainment giant Paramount Skydance (PSKY) may soon be nearly half foreign-owned, if the merger between itself and Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) concludes successfully. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) recently approved Paramount's own petition to be 49.5% owned by foreign entities. This did not sit well with investors, meanwhile, who sent Paramount shares down over 3% in the closing minutes of Thursday's trading. Paramount has seen a 43.87% loss in its share price over the past year.

Mother May I?

The biggest issue here was that Paramount owns 28 television stations. This requires the FCC to step in and approve a request for foreign entities to own anything more than 25% of the operation. And given that Paramount's move to acquire Warner is supported by the sovereign wealth funds of three different Gulf State entities, that meant a lot more than 25% was going to be owned by those funds.

The FCC noted that it was "…persuaded by Paramount's argument that the Foreign Investors therefore will not be able to wield any influence, let alone control, over decisions involving the Licensees." Given that 100% of voting stock will be held by the Ellison family and RedBird Capital Partners, this limited the foreign ownership stake to more of a silent partner position. Concern about the deal, of course, still emerged regardless of the FCC's stance.

What About the Indies?

Independent film has not been taking the move to streaming well. While once, the presence of video stores ensured sales of physical discs for a wide range of independent film titles, the rise of the streaming market has not done so well for the indie market. Some believe that indies will continue to suffer under a merged Paramount and Warner.

AGC chairman and CEO Stuart Ford penned a column for Deadline, noted that the independent film sector seems to be a non-starter in the Warner/Paramount deal altogether. Much of the complaint is focused on theater chains, streaming companies, and cable distributors. Indie film's presence in those complaints is nowhere to be seen, Ford asserted.

data.title: Apple Stock (AAPL): iPhone Survey Points to 28% Higher Average Selling Price
data.description:
Tech giant Apple (AAPL) could be heading into a stronger-than-usual iPhone upgrade cycle, according to Evercore ISI's latest consumer survey. The investment firm surveyed nearly 4,000 people and found that the expected average selling price, or ASP, reached $1,374. That is nearly 28% higher and well above Evercore's long-term survey average. Five-star analyst Amit Daryanani, who is ranked #14 out of 12,512 Wall Street analysts, also believes that iPhone pricing could rise more than 20% due to higher prices and greater demand for expensive models with more memory.

In fact, 53% of respondents said they plan to buy an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max. Evercore's historical average is 51%.

The Pro Max showed an even bigger move toward premium models. About 32% of consumers said they plan to buy the Pro Max, compared with 29% in last year's survey.

Apple's new iPhone Duo also appears to be attracting interest. About 14% of respondents said they plan to buy one. Last year, only 9% said they intended to buy the then-new iPhone Air.

More Apple Users Are Planning to Upgrade

Separately, the survey suggests that more existing users are ready to replace their phones. About 61% of respondents said that they plan to purchase an iPhone this year. That is up from 59% last year and is actually the second-highest reading in Evercore's survey history. It is also far above the firm's long-term average of 45%.

That stronger upgrade interest is worth noting because Apple could benefit from both higher unit demand and higher prices at the same time. If more buyers choose Pro models or larger memory configurations, revenue could rise faster than unit sales alone would suggest. The survey also found a small increase in consumers who plan to upgrade their Apple Watch and AirPods.

Therefore, Evercore sees the potential for Apple to surprise to the upside compared to Wall Street revenue expectations for Fiscal 2027, which sit near 7% growth. Daryanani also kept his Buy rating and raised his Apple price target to $380 from $365.
